claim: OECD and FAO project that the world's average intake of calories from meat, dairy, eggs and fish will rise by 6% per person over 2025 to 2034, and by 24% in lower-middle-income countries.
unit: percent change in per capita calorie intake from livestock and fish products
quote: global per capita calorie intake of livestock and fish products will increase by 6 percent over the next decade
notes: Second quote: 'growth is anticipated to reach 24 percent, nearly four times faster than the global average'. The Executive Summary (PRB-05) as read gives 25% for the same group; we report the press figure and flag the one-point gap for a checker. Projection (baseline), not a forecast of what must happen.

claim: The same Outlook projects world output of meat, dairy and eggs to grow by 17% to 2034, while herds of cattle, sheep, pigs and poultry grow by only 7%.
quote: the output of meat, dairy products and eggs is set to increase by 17 percent
notes: Second quote: 'total global inventories of cattle, sheep, pigs and poultry will expand by 7 percent'. The gap reflects expected productivity gains per animal.

claim: India and Southeast Asia are projected to supply 39% of the growth in world food consumption to 2034, up from 32% in the past decade, while China's share falls from 32% to 13%.
quote: India and Southeast Asian countries are projected to account for 39 percent of global consumption growth by 2034
notes: Applies to agricultural and fish commodities in total, not only protein. Useful to place Vietnam inside the region where demand growth now concentrates.

claim: The newest edition of the Outlook (2026 to 2035) projects world agricultural and fish production to grow 13% over ten years, with direct agricultural greenhouse gas emissions up 6%.
quote: Global production is projected to expand by 13% over the next ten years
notes: Second quote: 'Direct agricultural greenhouse gas emissions are expected to increase by 6%'. Read from the OECD landing page only; the report PDF is blocked to automated fetching (robots.txt) and the chapter pages render without text, so animal-product detail for 2035 was not read. The package holds the 2026 to 2035 data via the SDMX API (QNT-01).

claim: FAO's long-term projection is that demand for meat, milk and eggs from land animals will rise by about 20% between the 2020s and 2050.
unit: percent increase in demand for terrestrial animal products
quote: a projected 20 percent increase in demand for terrestrial animal products by 2050
notes: Base year not stated in the press release (the report's reference year for emissions is 2015). Much lower than FAO's 2011 projection (next fact); the two are not averaged.

claim: An older FAO projection (2011) expected meat consumption to rise by nearly 73% and dairy by 58% by 2050, a much steeper path than FAO's 2023 estimate.
quote: Meat consumption is projected to rise nearly 73 percent by 2050
notes: World Livestock 2011 press release, 14 Dec 2011. Different base year, population path and model from the 2023 figure of about 20% for all terrestrial animal products. Shows how long-range demand projections have been revised down; the often-repeated claim that protein demand will 'double by 2050' is not supported by either FAO figure.

claim: Two countries dominate the world's soybean exports: in marketing year 2024/25 Brazil shipped about 56% and the United States about 28%, together about 84%.
quote: Table values read (Mt, MY2024/25): world exports 184.330; Brazil 103.142; United States 51.495
notes: Shares are our division of USDA figures. USDA estimates for 2025/26: Brazil 115.0 of 187.2 Mt (61%), United States 41.4 Mt (22%), combined 84%. Vietnam's own soybean imports are 45.8% Brazil and 43.6% US (ch01).

claim: Much of the feed trade passes through a few sea lanes: over a quarter of world soybean exports transit the Strait of Malacca, and 54% of traded grain and fertiliser passed at least one maritime chokepoint in 2015.
quote: over a quarter of world soybean exports transit Malacca (package wording, app-x X.1.7)
notes: Reused from the package (app-x-drivers-signals). Chatham House think-tank report; older data.

claim: Protein feed prices can spike: the world fishmeal price reached about USD 2,500 per tonne in August 2026, up 43% on a year earlier.
unit: USD per tonne; percent year on year
quote: Fishmeal peak (Aug 2026): USD 2,500 per t (up 43% year on year) (package shock register SHK-014)
notes: Reused from package app-x X.11. El Nino years reprice aquafeed.

claim: Animal disease can remove a large share of supply at once: African swine fever killed or forced the culling of about 40% of China's pigs in 2018 to 2019.
quote: ASF in China (2018 to 2019): About 40% of China's pigs (as cited) (package shock register SHK-002)
notes: Figure as cited in a Vietnam ASF paper; the package labels it 'as cited'. Vietnam lost nearly 6 million pigs (over 20% of the herd) in 2019 (GEO-14, GEO-15).

claim: Bird flu (H5N1) jumped into US dairy cattle in 2024 and spread to more than 1,000 herds, with 71 human cases recorded in the US since February 2024.
quote: H5N1 in US dairy cattle (from 2024): Over 1,000 herds; 71 human cases (package shock register SHK-007)
notes: Reused from package. CDC rates the public risk 'low' (GEO-23). Science paper (GEO-21) traces it to a single spillover spread by cattle movement.

claim: About 36% of the calories produced by the world's crops go to animal feed, and only about 12% of those feed calories come back as human food.
unit: percent of crop calories; percent of feed calories returned as food
quote: only 12% of those feed calories ultimately contribute to the human diet
notes: Preceding words: '36% of the calories produced by the world's crops are being used for animal feed'. Put another way, about 4% of crop calories reach people as animal products (paper's own figure). Calorie basis only; protein and micronutrient quality of animal foods is not counted. Data are about 25 years old.

claim: The same study estimates that growing crops only for direct human consumption could raise available food calories by up to 70%, enough in principle for about 4 billion more people.
quote: could, in principle, increase available food calories by as much as 70%, which could feed an additional 4 billion people
notes: Theoretical upper bound: counts biofuel and other uses too, assumes all feed crops are edible and ignores grassland and by-products (see Mottet et al. 2017).

claim: OECD and FAO project that by 2034 a third (33%) of the world's cereals will be fed to animals, against 40% eaten directly by people.
quote: By 2034, 40 percent of all cereals will be consumed directly by humans, while 33 percent will be used for animal feed
notes: Cereals only; soybean meal, the main protein feed, is not included in this share.

claim: Meat, farmed fish, eggs and dairy use about 83% of the world's farmland but provide 37% of its protein and 18% of its calories.
unit: percent of farmland; of protein; of calories
quote: use ~83% of the world's farmland ... despite providing only 37% of our protein and 18% of our calories
notes: Confirms the task's figures. FAO gives livestock 34% of global food protein supply (PRB-17): different scope (FAO excludes farmed fish) and year, so both stand.

claim: In the same model, a world without animal products would need 76% less land for food (3.1 billion hectares) and emit 49% less food-related greenhouse gas (6.6 Gt CO2e).
quote: reducing food's land use by 3.1 (2.8-3.3) billion hectares (a 76% reduction)
notes: Second quote: 'food's GHG emissions by 6.6 (5.5-7.4) billion metric tons of CO2eq (a 49% reduction)'. A thought experiment, not a policy proposal; assumes plant foods replace animal foods nutritionally.

claim: Per 100 g of protein, the global average footprint of beef from beef herds is about 50 kg CO2e, lamb about 20, farmed prawns about 18, cheese about 11, pork 7.6, farmed fish 6.0, poultry 5.7, eggs 4.2, tofu 2.0, peas 0.44 and nuts 0.26.
unit: kg CO2e per 100 g protein (global mean)
quote: Beef (beef herd): 49.889668 ... Peas: 0.4410441 ... Tofu: 1.975 (OWID grapher CSV)
notes: These are the global MEANS that Our World in Data publishes (its metadata calls them 'global average'), not medians. Means are pulled up by a few high-impact producers. Nuts are low because tree planting stores carbon in some systems. Full table in data_protein_footprints.csv.

claim: Using medians instead of means, the typical footprint per 100 g of protein is about 25 kg CO2e for beef, 20 for lamb, 10 for farmed prawns, 8.4 for cheese, 6.5 for pork, 4.3 for poultry, 3.8 for eggs, 3.5 for farmed fish, 1.6 for tofu, 0.8 for nuts and 0.4 for peas.
unit: kg CO2e per 100 g protein (global median)
quote: The median footprint for beef is 25 kgCO2eq.
notes: Global medians from Poore and Nemecek as reported by Our World in Data (Ritchie 2020). Beef 25 is in the body text; lamb ('around 20'), prawns ('about 10') and the others were read from the article's chart description, so they are rounded. The paper's own Figure 1 values could not be extracted as text. Medians and means differ a lot (beef 25 vs 50); report both, never average.

claim: Footprints vary widely within each food, yet even low-impact animal products usually emit more than plant proteins: the lowest-impact 10% of beef emits about 9 kg CO2e per 100 g protein and lamb 12, while the highest-impact peas emit 0.8, nuts 2.4 and tofu 3.5.
unit: kg CO2e per 100 g protein (10th or 90th percentile)
quote: All are several times less than the lowest impact lamb (12 kgCO2eq) and beef (9 kgCO2eq).
notes: Paper's wording: 'the impacts of the lowest-impact animal products exceed average impacts of substitute vegetable proteins'. At the top end, 90th-percentile beef is 105 kg CO2e and 370 m2 of land per 100 g protein (PRB-01). Low-impact poultry, eggs and farmed fish overlap with high-impact tofu.

claim: Per 100 g of protein, beef from beef herds uses on average about 164 m2 of land for a year and lamb about 185 m2, against about 40 for cheese, 11 for pork, 7 for poultry, 6 for eggs, 4 for farmed fish, 2 for farmed prawns, 3 for peas and 2 for tofu.
unit: m2 x year per 100 g protein (global mean)
quote: Beef (beef herd): 163.5958 ... Lamb & Mutton: 184.81259 ... Tofu: 2.2 (OWID grapher CSV)
notes: Global means; land use counts area times years occupied and includes grazing land that often cannot grow crops (see Mottet et al.). Farmed prawns and fish look low on land because much of their feed and pond area is not counted as agricultural land in this dataset. Nuts 7.9.

claim: Food systems, from farm to plate, emitted about 18 Gt CO2e in 2015, about 34% of all human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, with 71% of that from farming and land-use change.
unit: Gt CO2e; percent of global GHG; percent of food-system GHG
quote: In 2015, food-system emissions amounted to 18 Gt CO2 equivalent per year globally, representing 34% of total GHG emissions.
notes: Covers all food, plant and animal. Scite indexes this paper under wrong author names; the correct authors are Crippa, Solazzo, Guizzardi, Monforti-Ferrario, Tubiello and Leip (checked on nature.com).

claim: FAO's latest estimate is that livestock supply chains emitted about 6.2 Gt CO2e in 2015, around 12% of human-caused emissions, with cattle responsible for 62%.
unit: Gt CO2e; percent of anthropogenic GHG; percent from cattle
quote: accounted for approximately 6.2 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent emissions (GtCO2eq) per year, equal to around 12 percent of all anthropogenic GHG emissions
notes: Second quote: 'cattle...contribute around 3.8 GtCO2 equivalent per year, or 62 percent of the livestock total'. FAO press release 8 Dec 2023 for the report 'Pathways towards lower emissions' (report PDF blocked to fetching).

claim: FAO's earlier and still widely quoted estimate was 7.1 Gt CO2e, or 14.5% of human-caused emissions, for the reference year 2005.
unit: Gt CO2e; percent of anthropogenic GHG
quote: With emissions estimated at 7.1 gigatonnes CO2-eq per annum, representing 14.5 percent of human-induced GHG emissions
notes: Reference year 2005 ('the year with the most recent complete set of data'). Cattle 4.6 Gt, 65%. Why 14.5% and 12% differ: different reference years (2005 vs 2015) and model versions (GLEAM 3 uses 2015, per FAO's GLEAM page), so the fall is not evidence that emissions went down. FAO's own stated reasons were not found in the release; updated emission factors, warming potentials and a larger world total are likely but unverified. Give both with their years; do not average.

claim: Without further action, FAO expects livestock emissions to reach nearly 9.1 Gt CO2e by 2050 if demand grows as projected.
quote: Without interventions and productivity gains, meeting increased demand is likely to bring global livestock emissions to nearly 9.1 GtCO2eq by 2050
notes: Projection. FAO's own report argues mainly for productivity and on-farm mitigation, with diet change as one lever among several.

claim: Farm animals were given an estimated 99,500 tonnes of antimicrobials in 2020, projected to rise 8% to about 107,500 tonnes by 2030.
quote: global AMU (tonnes) for cattle, sheep, chicken, and pigs was estimated at 99,502 tonnes of active ingredient
notes: 95% CI very wide: 68,535 to 193,052 t in the results text (the abstract prints 198,052; a typo in one place). Six of the ten largest meat producers, Vietnam included, do not publish use data, so the figure is modelled.

claim: Animals accounted for about 73% of all antimicrobials used worldwide in 2017, and Asia used 59% of the animal total in 2020.
unit: percent of global antimicrobial use; percent of animal use in Asia
quote: In 2017, antimicrobial use (AMU) in animals represented 73% of all antimicrobials used worldwide
notes: The 73% is cited by Mulchandani et al. from earlier work (Tiseo et al. 2020); not re-derived here. Asia 58,377 t (59%), China alone 32,776 t.

claim: In Vietnam about 71.7% of antimicrobials used in 2015 went to animals.
quote: About 71.7% of antimicrobials used in Vietnam in 2015 went to animals (package app-x X.2.3)
notes: Reused from package. Vietnam banned growth promoters from 2018 and allows antibiotics only to treat diagnosed disease from 1 Jan 2026 (GEO-24).

claim: About 60% of the 335 new human infectious diseases that emerged between 1940 and 2004 came from animals, but about 72% of those came from wild animals rather than farm animals.
unit: percent of emerging infectious disease events; percent of zoonotic events from wildlife
quote: EID events are dominated by zoonoses (60.3% of EIDs): the majority of these (71.8%) originate in wildlife
notes: Important for balance: the zoonosis argument applies to livestock mainly as a bridge or amplifier host (for example pigs for Nipah, poultry for H5N1), not as the main source. Counts events, not deaths.

claim: A 2020 UN Environment Programme and ILRI report named rising demand for animal protein and intensive, unsustainable farming among seven drivers of new zoonotic diseases, and said neglected zoonoses kill about two million people a year.
quote: increased demand for animal protein
notes: Second quote: 'Every year, some two million people, mostly in low- and middle-income countries, die from neglected zoonotic diseases.' Read via the UN country-team copy of the press release; the UNEP page returned 404. No numeric attribution of risk to livestock.

claim: The WHO cancer agency (IARC) classifies processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A); each 50 g of processed meat eaten daily raises colorectal cancer risk by about 18%.
unit: percent higher colorectal cancer risk per 50 g/day processed meat
quote: every 50 gram portion of processed meat eaten daily increases the risk of colorectal cancer by about 18%
notes: WHO stresses the groups describe strength of evidence (hazard), not size of risk, and that 'Meat can be part of a healthy diet'. For red meat, 17% per 100 g a day only if causal. Relevant to processed alternatives too: the classification concerns the meat, not processing in general.

claim: About 86 billion land animals were slaughtered for meat in 2024, of which about 78.5 billion (91%) were chickens; pigs numbered about 1.5 billion and cattle about 305 million.
notes: Our sum of FAOSTAT counts via Our World in Data for cattle, goats, chickens, turkeys, pigs, sheep and ducks (4.2 billion ducks). Excludes geese, rabbits, buffalo and others, so it is a floor. Motivation held by some actors (package framing).

claim: Estimates for fish are far larger and far less certain: roughly 1.1 to 2.2 trillion wild fish caught a year (2000 to 2019 average) and 78 to 171 billion farmed fish killed in 2019.
unit: trillion wild fish a year; billion farmed fish
quote: 1.1-2.2 trillion wild fishes were caught annually, on average, during 2000-2019
notes: Second quote: '124 billion farmed fishes were killed for food in 2019 (range 78-171 billion)'. Also 250 to 600 billion farmed crustaceans (2017). Fishcount.org.uk is an animal-welfare advocacy project; estimates derive FAO tonnage divided by assumed weights. Label Low.

claim: The United States launched a national biotechnology and biomanufacturing initiative by executive order in September 2022, directing the agriculture department to assess biotech for food and farming.
quote: The economic activity derived from biotechnology and biomanufacturing is referred to as 'the bioeconomy.'
notes: EO 14081, 12 Sep 2022. Also: USDA to assess 'how to use biotechnology and biomanufacturing for food and agriculture innovation'. Whether the order remains in force after the 2025 change of administration was not verified. US federal alternative-protein funding was about USD 11 M in 2025, down from about USD 115 M in 2024 (ECF-43, advocacy). A 2025 congressional commission recommended USD 15 billion for biotechnology but gave agriculture limited attention (ECF-42).

claim: China's first bioeconomy plan (May 2022) set a goal of 22 trillion yuan of bioeconomy output by 2025 and called for research on new foods such as 'artificial protein'.
quote: new food like artificial protein to lower the environmental and resources pressure arising from traditional breeding industries
notes: Read via Global Times (state-owned press), not the NDRC text. Whether 22 trillion is in the plan itself or a press gloss was not checked. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026 to 2030) names biomanufacturing a future industry (ECF-29).

claim: Other governments frame alternative protein as part of a wider bioeconomy: India targets a USD 300 billion bioeconomy by 2030 (from USD 165.7 billion in 2024) with 'smart proteins' a named area, and Japan targets a JPY 100 trillion bioeconomy market by 2030.
quote: Bioeconomy USD 165.7 bn (2024) to USD 300 bn (2030); smart proteins a named area (package bioeconomy_strategies BES-013)
notes: Government targets, not measured outcomes or forecasts with a published method. Reused from the package.

claim: Governments committed at least USD 2.5 billion of public money to alternative protein in 2021 to 2025, across 33 countries, according to an advocacy group.
quote: At least USD 2.5 bn cumulative (2021 to 2025) vs about USD 0.7 bn (2021); 33 countries engaged vs 16 (package BES-023)
notes: GFI is an advocacy group; totals depend on what it counts as protein diversification. Reused from package.

claim: FAO says livestock supports the livelihoods of at least 1.3 billion people and makes up about 20% of agricultural output in developing countries and 40% in developed ones.
unit: billion people; percent of agricultural output
quote: supporting the livelihoods of at least 1.3 billion people worldwide
notes: FAO web page, undated; the 1.3 billion figure is long-standing and its method is not given on the page. Same page: 'Thirty-four percent of global food protein supply comes from livestock.'

claim: FAO's 2023 review concludes that meat, eggs and milk supply high-quality protein and hard-to-get nutrients such as iron, zinc, vitamin B12 and calcium, which matter most for young children and pregnant women.
quote: High quality protein, a number of essential fatty-acids - together with iron, calcium, zinc, selenium, Vitamin B12, choline and bioactive compounds
notes: UN News report, 25 Apr 2023, of FAO 'Contribution of terrestrial animal source food to healthy diets'. The same report warns that even low intakes of processed red meat raise chronic disease risk.

claim: More than half of the world's preschool children (about 372 million) and 1.2 billion women of child-bearing age lack at least one of three key micronutrients, three quarters of the children in South and East Asia, the Pacific and sub-Saharan Africa.
quote: More than one in two preschool children (some 372 million) and 1.2 billion women of child-bearing age
notes: The three micronutrients are iron, zinc and vitamin A in FAO's framing (not verified beyond the UN News text). Argument against cutting animal foods where diets are poor; not an argument about rich-country diets.

claim: In low-income countries people eat on average only 143 kcal a day of animal-source food, and OECD-FAO project this will not rise by 2034, well below the 300 kcal FAO uses as a healthy-diet benchmark.
quote: In low-income countries, average daily per capita intake of animal-source foods is projected at 143 kcal, well below the 300-kcal benchmark
notes: Supports the view that some populations need more, not less, animal-source food. Vietnam is lower-middle income.

claim: Most of what livestock eat is not human food: 86% of global livestock feed (by dry matter) is grass, leaves, crop residues and by-products that people cannot eat.
unit: percent of livestock feed intake not edible by humans
quote: 86% is made of materials that are currently not eaten by humans
notes: Mottet et al. 2017 (FAO authors). Same abstract: livestock consume 6 billion t of feed dry matter a year and use about 2.5 billion ha. Still, livestock eat about one third of global cereals and need on average 2.8 kg (ruminants) and 3.2 kg (pigs and poultry) of human-edible feed per kg of boneless meat. Both this and Cassidy et al. are true: they measure different things (dry matter of all feed vs calories of crops).

claim: In a study of 118,397 UK adults, each extra 10% of daily energy from plant-based ultra-processed foods was linked to a 12% higher risk of dying from heart disease, while unprocessed plant foods were linked to 13% lower risk.
quote: plant-sourced UPF contribution was associated with a higher risk of mortality for all CVD (adjusted HR for 10% increase 1.12
notes: Observational; association not proof. 'Plant-sourced UPF' here is mostly packaged bread, pastries, biscuits, crisps and drinks, not mainly meat analogues. Widely reported in Vietnam as a finding about 'fake meat' (TRU-13). 95% CI 1.05 to 1.20 for the 1.12; non-UPF HR 0.87 (0.80 to 0.94).

claim: In a small randomised trial (36 US adults, 8 weeks each), eating plant-based meat instead of red meat lowered LDL cholesterol (110 vs 121 mg/dL) and TMAO, a marker linked to heart disease.
unit: mg/dL LDL cholesterol (plant vs animal phase)
quote: the Plant products improved several cardiovascular disease risk factors, including TMAO; there were no adverse effects on risk factors
notes: Small, short, no washout, and a significant order effect for TMAO. Funding source not verified here (reported elsewhere as an unrestricted gift from a plant-based meat company). Pair with the observational study above: trial and cohort evidence point different ways.

claim: Compared with the meat they imitate, plant-based meat products generally contain less protein, zinc and vitamin B12 and are often high in sodium, though they offer more fibre, less saturated fat and similar iron.
quote: plant-based meat alternative products generally contain less protein, zinc, and vitamin B12 than animal meats. Most also contain sodium in high amounts
notes: Narrative review built on a US audit of plant-based ground beef products. Iron in plants is non-heme and less absorbed, so 'similar iron' on the label overstates what the body gets (package app-j on phytate).

claim: A survey of 274 plant-based meat products in Hong Kong found them lower in energy, fat, saturated fat, protein and salt than the 151 meat products compared, but most were medium to high in fat and sugar by front-of-pack criteria.
quote: PBM had relatively lower energy density, total fat, saturated fat, protein, and salt compared to meat
notes: Nutritional verdicts depend on the comparator: against processed meat products, analogues look better on salt; against fresh meat (US study), worse. Give both.

claim: A peer-reviewed life-cycle assessment found near-term cultivated meat could emit 12 to 1,508 kg CO2e per kg; with pharmaceutical-grade purified growth media, 246 to 1,508 kg, which is 4 to 25 times the median for retail beef.
unit: kg CO2e per kg; times beef
quote: which is 4 to 25 times greater than the median GWP of retail beef
notes: Full sentence: all purified scenarios ranged from 246 to 1508 kg CO2e per kg; all scenarios 12 to 1508. Risner et al. 2024, the peer-reviewed version of the 2023 UC Davis preprint. Beef median about 60 kg CO2e per kg in their comparison. The low end (12 kg, food-grade media) is about 80% below median beef. The result turns on how refined the media must be, which is unresolved. Same paper: 1% of world meat would need about 30 times the 2021 world culture capacity (package app-v).

claim: Because cultivated meat's emissions are mostly long-lived carbon dioxide while cattle emit mostly short-lived methane, a 2019 climate-model study found cultivated meat is 'not prima facie climatically superior' to cattle; its advantage depends on clean energy.
quote: We conclude that cultured meat is not prima facie climatically superior to cattle production
notes: Lynch and Pierrehumbert 2019. In their high-energy case (about 360 MJ per kg), 25 kg per person a year for 10 billion people would need about 90 EJ, 22.9% of 2015 world energy use. Optimistic footprints remain better than cattle even over 1,000 years.

claim: An industry-informed life-cycle study for 2030 found that with renewable energy cultivated meat would have a lower carbon footprint than beef and pork, similar to efficient chicken, and use far less farmland.
quote: Using renewable energy, the carbon footprint is lower than beef and pork and comparable to the ambitious benchmark of chicken
notes: Sinke et al. 2023 (CE Delft), with data from over 15 companies; a correction was published in June 2023. One co-author (E. Swartz) is, to our knowledge, at GFI (advocacy); funding not re-checked. The same paper: without renewables the footprint 'may be higher than pork'.

claim: The leading independent cost model found cultivated meat would cost about USD 37 per kg of wet cells in fed-batch plants and USD 51 in perfusion plants, and concluded its economics 'would likely preclude' affordability as food.
unit: USD per kg wet cell mass
scope: modelled plant, 6.8 to 6.9 kt a year
quote: would likely preclude (package app-j J science, quoting Humbird 2021)
notes: Humbird 2021, commissioned by Open Philanthropy. USD 663 million capital for 6.9 kt a year. Growth factor cost assumption is the main swing factor (package DG-104).

claim: In the United States, the most studied market, plant-based meat sales fell from USD 1.4 billion in 2021 to USD 1.0 billion in 2025 and its share of meat sales halved to about 0.7%, while plant milk kept about 13% of milk sales.
unit: USD billion; percent of meat dollar sales; percent of milk dollar sales
quote: US plant-based meat sales fell from USD 1.4 billion (2021) to USD 1.0 billion (2025) (package ch23-consumers)
notes: Reused from package (app-ag AG.1, ch23). Plant milk share was 16% in 2021, so it dipped rather than held perfectly steady. GFI is an advocacy group; the data are licensed SPINS scans.
